extracted.intended_audience: Readers and implementers of the Metamath language and databases; formal-logicians and mathematicians constructing formal systems (e.g., Metamath set.mm authors).
extracted.subtask_description: Specifying and encoding a formal logical system and its proofs in the Metamath language (including example systems such as propositional calculus, predicate calculus with equality, ZFC, class notation, and the MIU system). Covers syntax, wff formation, axioms, rules, distinct-variable restrictions, and proof encoding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicit specification of alphabet: CN, VR, T, Γ
rubrics_metrics.description: A formal system should explicitly specify its constant symbols (CN), variable symbols (VR), type/formation declarations (T), and the set Γ of axiomatic/pre-statements (axioms and rules).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples show CN and VR enumerated; T contains expressions like 'wff ϕ' and Γ consists of the reducts of pre-statements. In Metamath these correspond to $c/$v declarations and $f/$e/$a statements (see mapping entries).

rubrics_metrics.name: Unambiguous wff (well-formed formula) formation rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions of wff formation must be stated so substitutions allowed by the formal system are unambiguous (e.g., include parentheses or otherwise eliminate ambiguity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text warns against omitting parentheses (or relying on operator precedence) because expressions like ¬ϕ → ψ could be ambiguous. Polish prefix notation could avoid parentheses but at readability cost. Ensure wff syntax ties unambiguously to allowed substitutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between metavariables and expository-language variables
rubrics_metrics.description: Be explicit about which symbols are primitive metavariables of the formal system (members of VR) and which are metavariables used in the expository metalanguage (e.g., use different symbols α, β for expository metavariables).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The book emphasizes that φ, ψ used in examples are primitive symbols (constants) within the formal system, not metavariables of the exposition, and cautions about the differing conventions in other texts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of distinct-variable restrictions
rubrics_metrics.description: When formalizing predicate calculus, include distinct-variable restrictions as part of axioms/pre-statements where required (e.g., restrictions like {x,y} on axioms).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples show explicit distinct-variable sets attached to pre-statements. Distinct-variable restrictions are essential for certain axioms (e.g., ¬∀x¬x = y where x and y distinct) and affect provability and metalogical arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mapping of logical hypotheses to inferences
rubrics_metrics.description: Logical hypotheses of the form '(cid:96) w where w is a wff (with leading term 'wff' removed)' are treated as inferences and can be used to build hierarchies of provable statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text notes that inferences (except modus ponens) are not strictly part of propositional calculus but are convenient. Nonsense hypotheses (that cannot be eliminated) are irrelevant for proving theorems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling free/bound variables and proper substitution without primitives
rubrics_metrics.description: If free-variable and proper-substitution notions are not primitives, mimic them via logical hypotheses and equivalences: e.g., use (ϕ → ∀x ϕ) to express 'x not free in ϕ' in practice, and use ((x = y → ϕ) ∧ ∃x(x = y ∧ ϕ)) to represent the result of proper substitution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This avoids messy recursive primitive definitions and works in the Metamath-style formalization; the text explains subtle differences (e.g., 'effectively not free') and their consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Axiom and rule specification (including modus ponens and generalization)
rubrics_metrics.description: A formal system must enumerate axioms (schemata) and inference rules (e.g., modus ponens, generalization) precisely, including the form of hypotheses used by rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples list standard propositional axioms, modus ponens (MP), generalization (Gen), and how they appear as pre-statements and reducts; be explicit about the hypotheses each rule requires.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of auxiliary devices for predicates: ranks and Vs sequence
rubrics_metrics.description: When adding predicate symbols, associate each predicate α ∈ Pr with a rank rnk(α) (its arity) and use a fixed sequence Vs to supply individual metavariables for argument positions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The specification then adds wff extension axioms for α and equality axioms for each argument position derived from these constructs; the book gives the general case and the binary predicate special-case for clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metalogical completeness vs provability of simple metatheorems
rubrics_metrics.description: Define metalogical completeness: a system is metalogically complete if all 'simple metatheorems' (those provable by combining provable cases outside the system) are directly provable inside the system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text explains simple metatheorems, gives examples of provable and non-provable pre-statements in Example 2, and notes Example 3 is metalogically complete while Example 2 is not (without metatheoretic combination).

rubrics_metrics.name: Conservative extension requirement for definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: When extending a formal system with definitions (new symbols/connectives), the extension should be conservative: no wff of the original language that was not a theorem should become a theorem of the extended system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The recommended approach is to introduce new connectives and axioms that define them (e.g., ↔, ∧, ∨, ∃) such that the extension is conservative. The text argues this is nicer than adding 'is defined as' as a primitive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of '=' and '↔' to introduce abbreviations and definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce new logical abbreviations and defined terms by adding axioms that use ↔ (for wffs) or = (for abstraction terms) so they act as 'is defined as' without extra primitive predicates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example 4 shows axioms like ((ϕ ↔ ψ) → (ϕ → ψ)) and (∃x ϕ ↔ ¬∀x¬ϕ). For abstraction classes, use '=' to define new class terms (e.g., {A,B} = {x|(x = A ∨ x = B)}).

rubrics_metrics.name: Class abstraction and conservative justification
rubrics_metrics.description: When using class abstraction notation {x|—}, treat classes as abbreviations justified as conservative extensions (reference Takeuti & Zaring, Quine).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce class variables and class-formation axioms, define membership and equality (Ab, Eq, El axioms), and apply distinct-variable restrictions where appropriate to avoid dependency on dummy variables.

rubrics_metrics.name: Careful use of distinct-variable restrictions for definitions involving dummy variables
rubrics_metrics.description: When the right-hand side of a definition involves an individual (dummy) variable not present in the expression being defined, impose distinct-variable restrictions (e.g., 'x does not occur in A or B') so the definition is independent of the dummy variable used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is recommended for class and other definitions; the text gives examples and warns about potential dangers (e.g., deriving Extensionality) requiring justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metamath database structure: declarations then extended frames
rubrics_metrics.description: A Metamath database should be organized into initial constant and variable declarations followed by extended frames (each delimited by ${ and $}) containing $d, $f, $e and assert statements; any database can be converted to this form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The book recommends this simple form and explains how math symbol tokens map to representatives of CN and VR, and how each extended frame corresponds to a pre-statement of the formal system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mapping between Metamath source keywords and formal-system components
rubrics_metrics.description: In Metamath: $c/$v declare constants/variables; $d/$f/$e correspond to D, T, H in formal-system statements; $a is an axiomatic assertion (axiom), and $p is a provable assertion (provable statement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each extended frame corresponds to a pre-statement; a frame corresponds to a formal-system statement. The math symbol strings following keywords correspond to expressions or variable pairs as appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proofs must accompany $p statements and are machine-verifiable
rubrics_metrics.description: Every $p (provable) statement in a Metamath database must be accompanied by a proof (which tells the computer how to construct specific members of the closure).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The proof instructs the computer on constructing the closure member matching the $p statement; the internal proof is not an element of the abstract formal system but a verification artifact. Proofs may be compressed or uncompressed; '?' denotes an incomplete proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frame definition and usage
rubrics_metrics.description: A frame is a sequence of 0 or more disjoint-stmt and hypothesis-stmt statements (possibly interleaved with other non-assert statements) followed by one assert-stmt; it corresponds to a pre-statement of the formal system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This structural rule defines how to organize declarations and hypotheses into reusable frames in a Metamath database, aligning with the formal-system notion of pre-statements and closures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metamath lexical/tokenization and comment rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Tokens are longest-match sequences of printable non-whitespace ASCII characters except '$'; labels have restricted character sets; comments use '$( ... $)' (must be surrounded by whitespace) and do not nest; whitespace is skipped between tokens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The EBNF defines PRINTABLE-SEQUENCE, MATH-SYMBOL, LABEL, COMPRESSED-PROOF-BLOCK, and whitespace/comment behavior. Implementations should follow these rules; comments are not allowed to nest and require trailing WHITECHAR.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof compression and compressed-proof block format
rubrics_metrics.description: Metamath supports compressed proofs with '(' LABEL* ')' COMPRESSED-PROOF-BLOCK+ syntax; compressed-proof-block tokens are sequences of uppercase letters or '?' and represent compressed steps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proofs can be interspersed with comments. '?' in a proof marks an incomplete proof. Implementors should support both uncompressed (sequence of labels) and compressed forms per the EBNF.

rubrics_metrics.name: MIU system encoding requirements (example of formal-system encoding)
rubrics_metrics.description: When encoding toy systems like Hofstadter's MIU-system in Metamath, declare constants (M, I, U, |- , wff), declare variables representing wffs, declare $f wff x entries, define wff formation rules (empty sequence allowed, concatenation with M/I/U), assert axiom MI, and give rules I–IV as $e/$a entries with appropriate templates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The MIU example notes practicalities: Rules III and IV may not be uniquely applicable without wff-typing; Metamath provides features like EMPTY_SUBSTITUTION (must be set on to allow empty substitutions) and shows a worked proof of M U I I U to illustrate proof construction and display.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof verification semantics: proof constructs closure, not part of abstract system
rubrics_metrics.description: The proof text in Metamath is a mechanism to communicate to the computer how to construct members of the closure of the formal-system pre-statement; the abstract formal system cares only about the existence of these closure members.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thus proofs are implementation-level artifacts: the final constructed member of the closure is what corresponds to a provable statement; the proof itself is not part of the abstract statement.

rubrics_metrics.name: When extending with functions or infinite constructs, use metalogic or set theory
rubrics_metrics.description: If the formal system would require infinitely many primitives (e.g., infinitely many function symbols or predicates), define them metalogically under set theory rather than trying to represent them directly within a finite Metamath database.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text remarks Metamath databases are finite; to describe an infinite formal system indirectly formalize the expository metalogic in set theory (as done in the Appendix) rather than attempt direct infinite declarations.
